title: Plant Organ Systems

competencies.text: Explain plant organ interaction for material transport.

days.title: The Plant as a System
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

This week you will explain how plant organs interact to transport materials — water, minerals and food.

🌿 Two Main Systems

A plant has a root system (below ground) and a shoot system (stems, leaves, flowers, fruits). They depend on each other: roots need sugar made by leaves; leaves need water and minerals absorbed by roots.

OrganMain functions
RootsAbsorb water and minerals; anchor the plant; may store food (kamote, carrots)
StemSupports leaves toward light; transports materials; may store food (sugarcane)
LeavesPhotosynthesis; gas exchange through stomata; transpiration
FlowersReproduction — pollination and seed formation
FruitsProtect seeds and help spread them

🔗 Why "System"?

If one organ is damaged, the others suffer. A plant with cut roots wilts even in wet soil; a plant stripped of leaves cannot make food, so its roots slowly starve. Healthy growth depends on all organs working together.

✅ Quick Check

3 questions — read each explanation.

scenario.text: Which plant organ mainly absorbs water and minerals?

choices.label: Roots
Leaves
Flowers
Fruits

scenario.explanation: Root hairs give roots a large surface for absorbing water and dissolved minerals.

scenario.text: Kamote and cassava store food in which organ?

choices.label: Roots
Stems
Leaves
Flowers

scenario.explanation: Kamote and cassava are swollen storage roots that hold starch made in the leaves.

scenario.text: All the leaves of a young tree are eaten by caterpillars. Why may its roots eventually die?

choices.label: Roots stop receiving sugar made in the leaves
Roots begin making too much food by themselves
Caterpillars move down and eat the roots next
Leaves were the only organ that absorbed water

scenario.explanation: Roots cannot photosynthesize. They depend on sugar sent down from the leaves.

days.title: Xylem and Phloem
days.content:
💧 Vascular Tissues

XylemPhloem
CarriesWater and dissolved mineralsSugars (food) made in leaves
DirectionUpward only: roots → leavesBoth ways: from source to sink
CellsDead, hollow tubes with thick wallsLiving sieve-tube cells
Also doesSupports the plant (wood is xylem)Carries some hormones

🍬 Source and Sink

A source makes or releases sugar (mature leaves). A sink uses or stores it (roots, fruits, new shoots). In a mango tree during fruiting, sugar moves from leaves to the growing fruits.

🌳 Girdling

The phloem lies just under the bark; xylem is deeper (the wood). If a full ring of bark is removed (girdling), phloem is cut: water still goes up, but sugar can no longer reach the roots. The roots starve and the tree eventually dies.

🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each term to its meaning. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

match.why: It runs from roots to leaves.

match.right: Carries sugars from source to sink
match.why: It can move food up or down.

match.right: Part that makes or releases sugar
Part that uses or stores sugar
Pores for gas exchange and water loss
match.why: Guard cells open and close them.

match.right: Removing a ring of bark, cutting the phloem

days.title: How Water Climbs a Tree
days.content:
⬆️ The Transpiration Stream

  1. Roots absorb water by osmosis; minerals enter by active transport.
  2. Water moves into xylem and up the stem.
  3. In leaves, water evaporates from cells and escapes as vapor through stomata — this is transpiration.
  4. Evaporation creates a pull. Water molecules stick to each other (cohesion) and to xylem walls (adhesion), so a continuous column is pulled up — like sipping through a straw.

🌡️ What Changes the Rate?

ConditionTranspirationWhy
Hot, sunnyFasterMore evaporation
WindyFasterMoist air around leaves is blown away
HumidSlowerAir already full of water vapor
Dry soilSlowerStomata close to save water

If water is lost faster than roots absorb it, cells lose turgor (water pressure) and the plant wilts. Closing stomata saves water but also limits CO₂ intake, slowing photosynthesis.

🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Explain plant transport in real situations. Read every explanation. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

scenario.text: A farmer removes a complete ring of bark from a tree trunk. Months later the tree dies. Why?

choices.label: Phloem was cut, so sugar could not reach the roots
Xylem was cut, so water could not reach the leaves
Insects entered the wound and ate all of the leaves
The bark was the part that made the tree's food

scenario.explanation: Phloem lies just beneath the bark. Cutting it stops sugar transport, so roots starve; xylem deeper inside still carries water for a while.

scenario.text: On a hot, windy afternoon, a potted plant wilts even though it was watered in the morning. What BEST explains this?

choices.label: Transpiration was faster than water absorption
The plant stopped making any glucose
Wind pushed water back down into the soil
Sunlight turned the water in its leaves to sugar

scenario.explanation: Heat and wind speed up transpiration. When leaves lose water faster than roots supply it, cells lose turgor and the plant wilts.

scenario.text: White carnations are placed in water with blue food coloring. After a day the petals turn bluish. Which tissue carried the dye?

choices.label: Xylem
Phloem
Stomata
Root hairs

scenario.explanation: Colored water moved up the stem through the xylem along with the transpiration stream.

scenario.text: During fruiting, a mango tree sends most of its sugar to the fruits. In this case, the fruits are…

choices.label: Sinks receiving sugar through phloem
Sources sending sugar to the leaves
Sinks receiving water through phloem
Sources taking minerals from the roots

scenario.explanation: Fruits use and store sugar, so they are sinks. Phloem carries sugar from the leaves (sources) to them.

scenario.text: A plant in very dry soil closes its stomata at midday. What is the trade-off?

choices.label: It saves water but takes in less CO₂ for photosynthesis
It gains more water but loses all its stored sugar at once
It saves water and doubles its rate of photosynthesis
It loses water but takes in much more oxygen instead

scenario.explanation: Closed stomata reduce water loss, but CO₂ also enters through stomata, so photosynthesis slows.

days.title: Organs Working Together
days.content:
🔄 The Full Cycle

  1. Roots absorb water and minerals → xylem carries them up.
  2. Leaves use light, CO₂ and water to make sugar (photosynthesis).
  3. Phloem carries sugar to roots, fruits and growing tips.
  4. Roots use that sugar for respiration and growth — so they can keep absorbing water.

Each organ supports the others. Break any link, and the whole plant suffers.

🌾 Applications in Philippine Farming

  • Transplanting rice: farmers keep soil around roots to avoid damaging root hairs, which reduces transplant shock.
  • Watering in the early morning or late afternoon: less water is lost to evaporation and transpiration.
  • Mulching: keeps soil moist so roots can keep up with transpiration.
  • Fertilizer with N, P and K: supplies minerals carried by the xylem for leaf growth and fruiting.

🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Lab

3 lives, 6 keys. You need 70% (5 of 6). Read each explanation.

escape.text: Which vascular tissue carries water upward from the roots?

choices.label: Xylem
Phloem
Cuticle
Stomata

escape.explanation: Xylem vessels carry water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves.

choices.label: Loss of water vapor through the stomata
Movement of sugar from leaves to roots
Absorption of minerals by the root hairs
Making glucose from light and carbon dioxide

escape.explanation: Transpiration is evaporation of water from leaves, mainly through stomata; it pulls water up the xylem.

escape.text: Which property lets water form a continuous column in the xylem?

choices.label: Cohesion between water molecules
Water molecules repelling each other
Gravity pulling water up the stem
Sugar dragging water down to roots

escape.explanation: Water molecules attract each other (cohesion), so pulling at the top lifts the whole column.

escape.text: Why do farmers keep soil around seedling roots when transplanting?

choices.label: To protect the delicate root hairs
To keep the leaves from getting wet
To make the seedlings much heavier
To stop the seedlings from growing

escape.explanation: Root hairs absorb most of the water. Damaging them causes wilting (transplant shock).

escape.text: Which tissue carries sugar from leaves to a kamote root?

choices.label: Phloem
Xylem
Epidermis
Root cap

escape.explanation: Phloem carries sugars from sources (leaves) to sinks such as storage roots.

escape.text: Why is watering plants at noon on a hot day less efficient than in the early morning?

choices.label: More water evaporates before roots use it
Roots cannot absorb any water in the daytime
Water at noon is heavier and sinks too deep
Plants only drink water when it is dark

escape.explanation: High heat speeds evaporation from soil and leaves, wasting water. Cooler times let more reach the roots.
